title: How Does Your Phone Always Know the Exact Time?
sources: Quartz clock (Wikipedia) and watch references: most quartz watch / real-time-clock crystals are tuning-fork crystals vibrating at 32,768 Hz (2^15); typical quartz watches are accurate to about +/-15 seconds per month, i.e. a few seconds a week

Android Open Source Project 'Network time detection' (source.android.com, updated 2026-10-09): Android asks an NTP server (default time.android.com, Google Public NTP) over SNTP; SNTP assumes symmetric delays and the correct time lies in the middle of the network round trip; telephony is a lower-priority time origin

NIST news release (8 Mar 2016) and NIST 'Usage analysis of the National Internet Time Service' (2016): ITS servers derive time from the NIST atomic timescale (an ensemble of atomic clocks calibrated by NIST-F1/NIST-F2 cesium fountain clocks); the service receives over 12 billion (about 16 billion as of Jan 2016) time requests per day
BIPM SI brochure: the second is defined by the cesium-133 hyperfine transition frequency, 9,192,631,770 Hz ('over nine billion' ticks a second)

lines.text: How does your phone know the exact time,
even if you never set it?
Inside, there's a tiny quartz crystal
that wobbles thirty two thousand, seven hundred sixty eight times a second.
Your phone counts those wobbles like clock ticks,
but quartz drifts, a few seconds every week.
So it quietly asks a time server online,
and that server is set by atomic clocks,
where cesium atoms tick over nine billion times a second.
lines.caps: WHERE *CESIUM | ATOMS *TICK | OVER *9 BILLION | TIMES A *SECOND

lines.text: It even subtracts the travel time,
so you're right to a split second.
And one American time service alone
gets over twelve billion requests every day.
So your phone isn't really keeping time.
It's borrowing it, from an atom.
